arXiv:1410.2126v4 [math.AG] 05 Sep 2017

On the values of logarithmic residues along curves

Delphine Pol Address: D.Pol
Université d’Angers, Département de Mathématiques
LAREMA, CNRS UMR no6093
2 Bd Lavoisier
49045 Angers
France Email address: pol@math.univ-angers.fr
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We consider the germ of a reduced curve, possibly reducible. F.Delgado de la Mata proved that such a curve is Gorenstein if and only if its semigroup of values is symmetrical. We extend here this symmetry property to any fractional ideal of a Gorenstein curve. We then focus on the set of values of the module of logarithmic residues along plane curves or complete intersection curves, which determines and is determined by the values of the Jacobian ideal thanks to our symmetry Theorem. Moreover, we give the relation with Kähler differentials, which are used in the analytic classification of plane branches. We also study the behaviour of logarithmic residues in an equisingular deformation of a plane curve.

Key words and phrases:
logarithmic residues, duality, Gorenstein curves, values, equisingular deformations
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
14H20, 14B07, 32A27

1. Introduction

Let DD be the germ of a reduced hypersurface in (ℂn,0)(\mathbb{C}^{n},0) defined by f∈ℂ⁡{x¯}:=ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn}f\in\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}:=\mathbb{C}\left\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right\} and with ring 𝒪D=ℂ​{x¯}/(f)\mathscr{O}_{D}=\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}/(f). In his fundamental paper [Sai80], K.Saito introduces the notions of logarithmic vector fields, logarithmic differential forms and their residues. A logarithmic differential form is a meromorphic form on a neighbourhood of the origin in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} which has simple poles along DD and such that its differential also has simple poles along DD. A logarithmic qq-form ω\omega satisfies:

g​ω=d​ff∧ξ+η,g\omega=\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{f}\wedge\xi+\eta,

where g∈ℂ​{x¯}g\in\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\} does not induce a zero divisor in 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}, ξ\xi is a holomorphic (q−1)(q-1)-form and η\eta is a holomorphic qq-form. Then, the logarithmic residue resq​(ω)\mathrm{res}^{q}(\omega) of ω\omega is defined as the coefficient of d​ff\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{f}, that is to say:

resq​(ω)=(ξg)​ D∈ΩDq−1⊗𝒪DQ⁡(𝒪D),\mathrm{res}^{q}(\omega)=\mathchoice{{\left(\frac{\xi}{g}\right)\,\smash{\vrule height=6.00002pt,depth=2.12502pt}}_{\,D}}{{\left(\frac{\xi}{g}\right)\,\smash{\vrule height=6.00002pt,depth=2.12502pt}}_{\,D}}{{\left(\frac{\xi}{g}\right)\,\smash{\vrule height=4.20001pt,depth=1.4875pt}}_{\,D}}{{\left(\frac{\xi}{g}\right)\,\smash{\vrule height=3.0pt,depth=1.44028pt}}_{\,D}}\in\Omega^{q-1}_{D}\otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{D}}Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}),

with ΩDq−1\Omega^{q-1}_{D} the module of Kähler differentials on DD and Q⁡(𝒪D)Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) the total ring of fractions of 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}. We denote by ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} the 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}-module of logarithmic residues of logarithmic 11-forms.

In [GS14], M.Granger and M.Schulze prove that the 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}-dual of the Jacobian ideal of DD is ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}. If in addition DD is free, that is to say, if the module of logarithmic differential 11-forms is a free ℂ​{x¯}\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}-module, the converse also holds: the dual of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} is the Jacobian ideal. They use this duality to prove a characterization of normal crossing divisors in terms of logarithmic residues: if the module ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} is equal to the module of weakly holomorphic functions on DD then DD is normal crossing in codimension 11. The converse implication was already proved in [Sai80].

The purpose of this paper is to investigate more deeply the module of logarithmic residues. We focus on the case of plane curves or complete intersection curves. Plane curves are always free divisors, and they are the only singular free divisors with isolated singularities. The notion of multi-residues along complete intersections was introduced by A.G.Aleksandrov and A.Tsikh in [AT01].

In order to describe the module of residues, or more generally, any fractional ideal, we will consider the set of values, which is defined as follows. Let D=D1∪⋯∪DpD=D_{1}\cup\dots\cup D_{p} be the germ of a reduced complex analytic curve with pp irreducible components. The normalization of the local ring 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} induces a map val:Q⁡(𝒪D)→(ℤ∪{∞})p\mathrm{val}:Q(\mathscr{O}_{D})\to\left(\mathbb{Z}\cup\left\{\infty\right\}\right)^{p} called the value map, which associates with a fraction g∈Q⁡(𝒪D)g\in Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) the pp-uple of the valuations of gg along each irreducible component of DD. Given a fractional ideal I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) (see Definition 2.2), we denote by val⁡(I)\mathrm{val}(I) the set of values of the non zero divisors of II, and I∨:={g∈Q(𝒪D);g⋅I⊆𝒪D}I^{\vee}:=\left\{g\in Q(\mathscr{O}_{D});g\cdot I\subseteq\mathscr{O}_{D}\right\} the dual of II.

Let us explain the content of section 2. We prove that the values of a fractional ideal and the values of its dual determine each other, and we give explicitly the relation between them. We then apply this result to the case of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} and of the Jacobian ideal of DD, denoted by 𝒥D\mathscr{J}_{D}, in parts 3 and 4. This relation is in fact a generalization of the following well-known theorem of Kunz in the case of irreducible curves:

Theorem 1.1 ([Kun70]).

If DD is irreducible, 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} is Gorenstein if and only if the following property, which is called a symmetry property, is satisfied: for all v∈ℤv\in\mathbb{Z},

v∈val⁡(𝒪D)⇔γ−v−1∉val⁡(𝒪D),v\in\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D})\iff\gamma-v-1\notin\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D}),

where γ\gamma is the conductor of DD, that is to say, γ=min{α∈ℕ;α+ℕ⊆val(𝒪D)}\gamma=\min\left\{\alpha\in\mathbb{N};\alpha+\mathbb{N}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D})\right\}.

In [DdlM88, Theorem 2.8], F.Delgado de la Mata generalizes the former result to the case of reducible curves. He proves that a curve is Gorenstein if and only if val⁡(𝒪D)\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D}) satisfies a symmetry property described below.

We prove here that Delgado’s symmetry has an analogue which links the values of a fractional ideal and the values of its dual. Whereas the symmetry is immediate for irreducible curves, the proof of this generalization of Delgado’s Theorem is much more subtle. It leads to the main result of this section, namely Theorem 1.2, which generalizes Theorem 2.4 of [Pol15] to any Gorenstein curve and any fractional ideal. To give the statement of our symmetry Theorem, we introduce the following notation for i∈{1,…,p}i\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\}, v∈ℤpv\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} and II a fractional ideal (see Notation 2.13):

Δi(v,val(I)):={α∈val(I);αi=vi,∀j≠i,αj>vj},\Delta_{i}(v,\mathrm{val}(I)):=\left\{\alpha\in\mathrm{val}(I);\alpha_{i}=v_{i},\forall j\neq i,\alpha_{j}>v_{j}\right\},

and Δ⁡(v,val⁡(I))=⋃i=1pΔi​(v,val⁡(I))\Delta(v,\mathrm{val}(I))=\bigcup_{i=1}^{p}\Delta_{i}(v,\mathrm{val}(I)). We consider the product order on ℤp\mathbb{Z}^{p}, that is to say, for α,β∈ℤp\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}, α⩽β\alpha\leqslant\beta means that for all i∈{1,…,p},αi⩽βii\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\},\alpha_{i}\leqslant\beta_{i}. The conductor of DD is: γ:=inf{α∈ℕp;α+ℕp⊆val(𝒪D)}\gamma:=\inf\left\{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{p};\alpha+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D})\right\}. We set 1¯=(1,…,1)\underline{1}=(1,\ldots,1). The statement of our main Theorem is:

Theorem 1.2.

Let DD be the germ of a reduced analytic curve with pp irreducible components. Then, the ring 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} of the curve is a Gorenstein ring if and only if for all fractional ideals I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) the following property is satisfied for all v∈ℤpv\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}:

(1) v∈val⁡(I∨)⇔Δ⁡(γ−v−1¯,val⁡(I))=∅.v\in\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee})\iff\Delta(\gamma-v-\underline{1},\mathrm{val}(I))=\emptyset.

Delgado’s Theorem concerns the case I=𝒪DI=\mathscr{O}_{D} (see Theorem 2.14). A similar symmetry was recently proved in [KST15] using combinatorial methods which involve canonical modules.

In part 3 and 4, we use Theorem 1.2 to study the module of logarithmic residues along complete intersection curves, with a particular attention to the case of plane curves.

In subsection 3.2, we give some properties of the set of values of the module of logarithmic residues and of the Jacobian ideal for plane curves. We investigate the zero divisors of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} and 𝒥D\mathscr{J}_{D}, which are described in Propositions 3.15 and 3.18. Thanks to our symmetry Theorem, we then determine the conductor of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}, which is −(m(1),…,m(p))+1¯-(m^{(1)},\ldots,m^{(p)})+\underline{1}, where m(i)m^{(i)} is the multiplicity of the branch DiD_{i}. We also mention the relation between logarithmic differential forms and the torsion of Kähler differentials. Thanks to this relation, we recover the result of O.Zariski on the dimension of the torsion of Kähler differentials, which is equal to the Tjurina number.

In subsection 3.3, we recall the theory of of multi-logarithmic differential forms and multi-residues along a reduced complete intersection developed by A.G.Aleksandrov and A.Tsikh in [AT01]. Since our symmetry Theorem is true for any Gorenstein curve, it is in particular true for complete intersection curves. As in the hypersurface case, we again have a duality between multi-residues and the Jacobian ideal, so that their sets of values determine each other. Moreover, we prove here the following proposition (see Proposition 3.31 for a more precise statement):

Proposition 1.3.

Let ΩC1\Omega^{1}_{C} be the module of Kähler differentials along a reduced complete intersection curve CC. The values of 𝒥C\mathscr{J}_{C} and the values of ΩC1\Omega^{1}_{C} satisfy:

val⁡(𝒥C)=γ+val⁡(ΩC1)−1¯.\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{J}_{C})=\gamma+\mathrm{val}(\Omega^{1}_{C})-\underline{1}.

The set of values of Kähler differentials is a major ingredient used in [HH11] and [HHH15] to study the problem of the analytic classification of plane curves with one or two branches.

The last section is devoted to the study of the behaviour of logarithmic residues in an equisingular deformation of a plane curve. In particular, we define a stratification by the values of the logarithmic residues, which is the same as the stratification by Kähler differentials thanks to subsection 3.3. We prove that this stratification is finer than the stratification by the Tjurina number. We give an example in which the stratification by logarithmic residues is strictly finer than the stratification by the Tjurina number (see Example 4.16). We show that the stratification by logarithmic residues is finite and constructible (see Propositions 4.14 and 4.15). We also give an example in which the frontier condition is not satisfied (see Example 4.19).

2. The symmetry of values

This section is devoted to the main Theorem 1.2, which is a generalization of the symmetry Theorem 2.8 of [DdlM88].

We first recall several properties of fractional ideals and the notion of conductor of a curve. We then introduce some definitions and notations inspired by [DdlM88] which appear in the statement of the main Theorem 1.2. We give in subsection 2.2 a detailed proof of this Theorem, and then a property of the Poincaré series associated with a fractional ideal of a Gorenstein curve (see Proposition 2.34).

2.1. Properties of fractional ideals

We recall some basic results on the fractional ideals of a curve. In particular, we give several properties of the set of values of a fractional ideal, and we define its dual.

Let DD be the germ of a reduced complex analytic curve, with pp irreducible components D1,…,DpD_{1},\ldots,D_{p}. The ring 𝒪Di\mathscr{O}_{D_{i}} of the branch DiD_{i} is a one-dimensional integral domain, so that its normalization 𝒪D~i\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}_{i}} is isomorphic to ℂ​{ti}\mathbb{C}\left\{t_{i}\right\} (see for example [dJP00, Corollary 4.4.10]). By the splitting of normalization (see [dJP00, Theorem 1.5.20]), the ring 𝒪D~\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}} of the normalization of DD is 𝒪D~=⨁i=1pℂ⁡{ti}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{C}\left\{t_{i}\right\}. Moreover, the total rings of fractions Q⁡(𝒪D)Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) of 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} and Q⁡(𝒪D~)Q(\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}) of 𝒪D~\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}} are equal (see [dJP00, Exercise 4.4.16]). We then have :

Q⁡(𝒪D~)=Q⁡(𝒪D)=⨁i=1pQ⁡(ℂ⁡{ti}).Q(\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}})=Q(\mathscr{O}_{D})=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{p}Q(\mathbb{C}\left\{t_{i}\right\}).
Definition 2.1.

Let g∈Q⁡(𝒪D)g\in Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}). We define the valuation of gg along the branch DiD_{i} as the order of tit_{i} of the image of gg by the surjection map Q⁡(𝒪D)→Q⁡(ℂ⁡{ti})Q(\mathscr{O}_{D})\to Q(\mathbb{C}\left\{t_{i}\right\}). We denote the valuation of gg along DiD_{i} by vali​(g)∈ℤ∪{∞}\mathrm{val}_{i}(g)\in\mathbb{Z}\cup\left\{\infty\right\}, with the convention vali​(0)=∞\mathrm{val}_{i}(0)=\infty.

We then define the value of gg by val⁡(g):=(val1​(g),…,valp​(g))∈(ℤ∪{∞})p\mathrm{val}(g):=\left(\mathrm{val}_{1}(g),\ldots,\mathrm{val}_{p}(g)\right)\in\left(\mathbb{Z}\cup\left\{\infty\right\}\right)^{p}.

Definition 2.2.

Let I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) be an 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}-module. We call II a fractional ideal if II is of finite type over 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} and if II contains a non zero divisor of Q⁡(𝒪D)Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}). We set:

val⁡(I):={val⁡(g);g∈I​ non zero divisor }⊂ℤp\mathrm{val}(I):=\left\{\mathrm{val}(g);g\in I\text{ non zero divisor }\right\}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{p}

and

val⁡(I)¯:={val⁡(g);g∈I}⊂(ℤ∪{∞})p.\overline{\mathrm{val}(I)}:=\left\{\mathrm{val}(g);g\in I\right\}\subset\left(\mathbb{Z}\cup\left\{\infty\right\}\right)^{p}.
Remark 2.3.

We will prove in section 3 that for a fractional ideal II, the set val⁡(I)\mathrm{val}(I) determines the set val⁡(I)¯\overline{\mathrm{val}(I)} (see Proposition 3.11).

Definition 2.4.

Let I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) be a fractional ideal. The dual of II is:

I∨:=Hom𝒪D​(I,𝒪D).I^{\vee}:=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathscr{O}_{D}}\left(I,\mathscr{O}_{D}\right).
Remark 2.5.

We also have I∨≃{g∈Q⁡(𝒪D);g​I⊆𝒪D}I^{\vee}\simeq\left\{g\in Q(\mathscr{O}_{D});gI\subseteq\mathscr{O}_{D}\right\} (see for example [dJP00, Proof of Lemma 1.5.14]).

Lemma 2.6.

The dual I∨I^{\vee} of a fractional ideal II is also a fractional ideal. Moreover, if I,JI,J are two fractional ideals satisfying J⊆IJ\subseteq I, then J∨⊇I∨J^{\vee}\supseteq I^{\vee}.

The conductor ideal of the curve DD is 𝒞D:=𝒪D~∨\mathscr{C}_{D}:=\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}^{\vee}.

Let DD be the germ of a reduced curve with pp irreducible components. Then, the ring 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} of the curve is a Gorenstein ring if and only if for all v∈ℤpv\in\mathbb{Z}^{p},

2.2. Proof of Theorem 1.2

The proof of Theorem 1.2 is developed in several steps. We first mention the implications which are easy consequences of [DdlM88] (see Lemma 2.15 and Proposition 2.18). The remain of this subsection is then devoted to the missing implication, which needs much more work (see subsections 2.2.2 and 2.2.3).

The following Lemma is a direct consequence of Theorem 2.14. Indeed, if the condition (1) is satisfied for all fractional ideals II, it is in particular satisfied by 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}.

Lemma 2.15.

Let DD be a reduced curve. If (1) is satisfied for all fractional ideals I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}), then 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} is Gorenstein.

Remark 2.16.

It is not sufficient to check if (1) is satisfied for one fractional ideal II to prove that the curve is Gorenstein. Indeed, by definition, for every curve, the equivalence (1) is satisfied by I=𝒪D~I=\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}} and I∨=𝒞DI^{\vee}=\mathscr{C}_{D}.

Our purpose now is to prove that for a Gorenstein curve and a fractional ideal I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}), property (1) is satisfied. Nevertheless, some of the properties we will prove or mentioned are also satisfied by non Gorenstein curves, so that we first consider an arbitrary reduced curve DD.

Let I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) be a fractional ideal. To prove the implication ⇒\Rightarrow of (1), we need the following result:

Proposition 2.17 ([DdlM88, Corollary 1.9]).

Let DD be a reduced curve. Then:

Δ⁡(γ−1¯,𝒪D)=∅.\Delta(\gamma-\underline{1},\mathscr{O}_{D})=\emptyset.
Proposition 2.18.

Let DD be a reduced curve. Let v∈ℤpv\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} and I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) be a fractional ideal. Then:

v∈val⁡(I∨)⇒Δ⁡(γ−v−1¯,I)=∅.v\in\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee})\Rightarrow\Delta(\gamma-v-\underline{1},I)=\emptyset.
Proof.

Let v=(v1,…,vp)∈val⁡(I∨)v=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{p})\in\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}), and g∈I∨g\in I^{\vee} with v=val⁡(g)v=\mathrm{val}(g). We assume Δ⁡(γ−v−1¯,I)≠∅\Delta(\gamma-v-\underline{1},I)\neq\emptyset. For the sake of simplicity, we may assume that Δ1​(γ−v−1¯,I)≠∅\Delta_{1}(\gamma-v-\underline{1},I)\neq\emptyset. It means that there exists h∈Ih\in I with val⁡(h)=(γ1−v1−1,w2,…,wp)∈val⁡(I)\mathrm{val}(h)=(\gamma_{1}-v_{1}-1,w_{2},\ldots,w_{p})\in\mathrm{val}(I) such that for all j⩾2j\geqslant 2, wj>γj−vj−1w_{j}>\gamma_{j}-v_{j}-1. Since g​h∈𝒪Dgh\in\mathscr{O}_{D}, we have (γ1−1,w2+v2,…,wp+vp)∈val⁡(𝒪D)(\gamma_{1}-1,w_{2}+v_{2},\ldots,w_{p}+v_{p})\in\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D}), with wj+vj⩾γjw_{j}+v_{j}\geqslant\gamma_{j}. Therefore, Δ1​(γ−1¯,𝒪D)≠∅\Delta_{1}(\gamma-\underline{1},\mathscr{O}_{D})\neq\emptyset.

Nevertheless, by Proposition 2.17, Δ⁡(γ−1¯,𝒪D)=∅\Delta(\gamma-\underline{1},\mathscr{O}_{D})=\emptyset, which leads to a contradiction. Therefore, Δ⁡(γ−v−1¯,I)=∅\Delta(\gamma-v-\underline{1},I)=\emptyset. ∎

Notation 2.19.

We set 𝒱={v∈ℤp;Δ⁡(γ−v−1¯,I)=∅}\mathscr{V}=\left\{v\in\mathbb{Z}^{p};\Delta(\gamma-v-\underline{1},I)=\emptyset\right\}.

Proposition 2.18 tells us that the set 𝒱\mathscr{V} contains the values of I∨I^{\vee}, but a priori it may be bigger. In particular, it is not obvious that 𝒱\mathscr{V} is the set of values of an 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}-module. Our purpose here is to prove that 𝒱\mathscr{V} is indeed equal to val⁡(I∨)\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}) when DD is Gorenstein.

Proposition 2.20.

Let DD be an irreducible Gorenstein curve. The statement of Theorem 1.2 can be rephrased as follows: for all v∈ℤv\in\mathbb{Z}, v∈val⁡(I∨)v\in\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}) if and only if γ−v−1∉val⁡(I)\gamma-v-1\notin\mathrm{val}(I).

Proof.

This proposition is a generalization of Kunz’s theorem 1.1. We have:

dimℂI∨/tγ−λ​ℂ​{t}\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I^{\vee}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathbb{C}\left\{t\right\} =Card⁡(val⁡(I∨)∩(γ−λ+ℕ)c)\displaystyle=\mathrm{Card}\left(\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee})\cap\left(\gamma-\lambda+\mathbb{N}\right)^{c}\right)
dimℂtλ​ℂ​{t}/I\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{C}}t^{\lambda}\mathbb{C}\left\{t\right\}/I =Card⁡((λ+ℕ)∩(val⁡(I))c)\displaystyle=\mathrm{Card}\big((\lambda+\mathbb{N})\cap\left(\mathrm{val}(I)\right)^{c}\big)

Since by Proposition 2.12, dimℂIν/tγ−λ​ℂ​{t}=dimℂtλ​ℂ​{t}/I\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I^{\nu}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathbb{C}\left\{t\right\}=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}t^{\lambda}\mathbb{C}\left\{t\right\}/I, we have the result. ∎

The proof for a reducible Gorenstein curve is based on a more intricate dimension argument.

2.2.1. Dimension and values

As we have seen in Proposition 2.20, it is easy to compute dimensions from the set of values in the irreducible case. The purpose of this subsection is to give a combinatorial method to compute some dimensions from the set of values.

Let v∈ℤpv\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}. We set Iv={g∈I;val⁡(g)⩾v}I_{v}=\left\{g\in I;\mathrm{val}(g)\geqslant v\right\} and ℓ⁡(v,I)=dimℂI/Iv\ell(v,I)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/I_{v}. Since 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} is one-dimensional, we have ℓ⁡(v,I)<∞\ell(v,I)<\infty.

We denote by (e1,…,ep)(e_{1},\ldots,e_{p}) the canonical basis of ℤp\mathbb{Z}^{p}. For ℰ⊆ℤp\mathscr{E}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{p} and v∈ℤpv\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}, let

Λi(v,ℰ)={α∈ℰ;αi=vi and α⩾v}.\Lambda_{i}(v,\mathscr{E})=\{\alpha\in\mathscr{E}\ ;\ \alpha_{i}=v_{i}\text{ and }\alpha\geqslant v\}.

We have the following inclusion: Δi​(v,ℰ)⊆Λi​(v,ℰ)\Delta_{i}(v,\mathscr{E})\subseteq\Lambda_{i}(v,\mathscr{E}). We then have (see [DdlM88, Proposition 1.11]):

Proposition 2.21.

For all v∈ℤpv\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}, ℓ⁡(v+ei,I)−ℓ⁡(v,I)=dimℂIv/Iv+ei∈{0,1}\ell(v+e_{i},I)-\ell(v,I)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I_{v}/I_{v+e_{i}}\in\{0,1\} and moreover ℓ⁡(v+ei,I)=ℓ⁡(v,I)+1\ell(v+e_{i},I)=\ell(v,I)+1 if and only if Λi​(v,val⁡(I))≠∅\Lambda_{i}(v,\mathrm{val}(I))\neq\emptyset.

Thanks to this proposition we can compute some dimensions from the set of values:

Corollary 2.22.

Let ν,λ∈ℤp\nu,\lambda\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} such that ν+ℕp⊆val⁡(I)⊆λ+ℕp\nu+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(I)\subseteq\lambda+\mathbb{N}^{p} (see Lemma 2.11). Let (α(j))0⩽j⩽M+1(\alpha^{(j)})_{0\leqslant j\leqslant M+1} be a finite sequence of elements of ℤp\mathbb{Z}^{p} with M=−1+∑i=1p(νi−λi)M=-1+\sum_{i=1}^{p}(\nu_{i}-\lambda_{i}), which satisfies:

  • •

    α(0)=λ\alpha^{(0)}=\lambda and α(M+1)=ν\alpha^{(M+1)}=\nu

  • •

    For all j∈{0,…,M}j\in\{0,\ldots,M\}, there exists i⁡(j)∈{1,…,p}i(j)\in\{1,\ldots,p\} such that α(j+1)=α(j)+ei⁡(j)\alpha^{(j+1)}=\alpha^{(j)}+e_{i(j)}

Then:

(6) dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~=ℓ⁡(ν,I)=Card⁡{j∈{0,…,M};Λi⁡(j)​(α(j),val⁡(I))≠∅}.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\ell(\nu,I)=\mathrm{Card}\left\{j\in\{0,\ldots,M\};\Lambda_{i(j)}(\alpha^{(j)},\mathrm{val}(I))\neq\emptyset\right\}.
Example 2.23.

The following example illustrates Corollary 2.22 for p=2p=2. We consider the plane curve DD defined by f⁡(x,y)=(x2−y3)​(x4−y3)f(x,y)=(x^{2}-y^{3})(x^{4}-y^{3}). A parametrization of this place curve is given by x=(t13,t23)x=(t_{1}^{3},t_{2}^{3}), y=(t12,t24)y=(t_{1}^{2},t_{2}^{4}). We consider the Jacobian ideal I=𝒥DI=\mathscr{J}_{D} of DD. In particular, val⁡(∂f∂x)=(9,15)\mathrm{val}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)=(9,15) and val⁡(∂f∂y)=(10,14)\mathrm{val}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)=(10,14). Therefore, by Proposition 2.9, we have (9,14)∈val⁡(𝒥D)(9,14)\in\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{J}_{D}). We represent by crosses the elements of II.

We can choose for example λ=(8,13)\lambda=(8,13) and ν=(13,21)\nu=(13,21). We consider the sequence α\alpha defined by the grey circles on figure 2. In particular, α(0)=λ\alpha^{(0)}=\lambda and α(13)=ν\alpha^{(13)}=\nu. The sets Λi⁡(j)​(α(j),val⁡(I))\Lambda_{i(j)}(\alpha^{(j)},\mathrm{val}(I)) for j∈{0,…,12}j\in\left\{0,\ldots,12\right\} corresponds to the crosses which are on the thick black lines. By the corollary, for this example, we have: dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~=7\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=7.

2.2.2. Preliminary steps

We recall that 𝒱={v∈ℤp;Δ⁡(γ−v−1¯,I)=∅}\mathscr{V}=\left\{v\in\mathbb{Z}^{p};\Delta(\gamma-v-\underline{1},I)=\emptyset\right\}, and this set contains val⁡(I∨)\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}). The purpose of this section is to show that if the inclusion val⁡(I∨)⊆𝒱\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee})\subseteq\mathscr{V} is strict, then it has some combinatorial and numerical consequences (see Lemma 2.26 and Proposition 2.27). We then prove in subsection 2.2.3 that these criteria lead to a contradiction in the Gorenstein case, which finishes the proof of Theorem 1.2.

First step

We first show that if 𝒱≠val⁡(I∨)\mathscr{V}\neq\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}), then there is an element w∈𝒱\val⁡(I∨)w\in\mathscr{V}\backslash\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}) which satisfies some properties which will be used in the next steps.

Let us assume that 𝒱≠val⁡(I∨)\mathscr{V}\neq\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}), and let w(0)∈𝒱\val⁡(I∨)w^{(0)}\in\mathscr{V}\backslash\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}) be "an intruder". By Lemma 2.11, there exist λ,ν∈ℤp\lambda,\nu\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} satisfying ν+ℕp⊆val⁡(I)⊆λ+ℕp\nu+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(I)\subseteq\lambda+\mathbb{N}^{p} and γ−ν⩽w(0)⩽γ−λ\gamma-\nu\leqslant w^{(0)}\leqslant\gamma-\lambda. For the remainder of the proof, we fix such λ,ν\lambda,\nu.

The following proposition gives an essential property of w(0)w^{(0)}:

Proposition 2.24.

There exists j∈{1,…,p}j\in\{1,\ldots,p\} such that Λj​(w(0),val⁡(I∨))=∅\Lambda_{j}(w^{(0)},\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}))=\emptyset. Moreover, the corresponding coordinate satisfies wj(0)<γj−λjw^{(0)}_{j}<\gamma_{j}-\lambda_{j}.

Proof.

If for all i∈{1,…,p}i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}, Λi​(w(0),val⁡(I∨))≠∅\Lambda_{i}(w^{(0)},\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}))\neq\emptyset, then for all i∈{1,…,p}i\in\{1,\ldots,p\} there exists α(i)∈val⁡(I∨)\alpha^{(i)}\in\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}) such that αi(i)=wi(0)\alpha^{(i)}_{i}=w^{(0)}_{i} and αj(i)⩾wj(0)\alpha^{(i)}_{j}\geqslant w^{(0)}_{j}. As a consequence, by Proposition 2.9, inf(α(1),…,α(p))=w(0)∈val⁡(I∨)\inf(\alpha^{(1)},\ldots,\alpha^{(p)})=w^{(0)}\in\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}), which is a contradiction. It gives the existence of a j∈{1,…,p}j\in\{1,\ldots,p\} such that Λj​(w(0),val⁡(I∨))=∅\Lambda_{j}(w^{(0)},\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}))=\emptyset. It is immediate to see that wj(0)<γj−λjw^{(0)}_{j}<\gamma_{j}-\lambda_{j} since if wj(0)=γj−λjw^{(0)}_{j}=\gamma_{j}-\lambda_{j}, then γ−λ∈Λj​(w(0),val⁡(I∨))\gamma-\lambda\in\Lambda_{j}(w^{(0)},\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee})), which contradicts the emptiness. ∎

Second step

For the sake of simplicity, we assume that Λp​(w(0),val⁡(I∨))=∅\Lambda_{p}(w^{(0)},\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}))=\emptyset. Corollary 2.22 together with a convenient finite sequence α\alpha can be used to compute the dimension of the quotient I∨/tγ−λ​𝒪D~I^{\vee}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}. We compare it with the number ℓ=Card⁡{j∈{0,…,n0−1};Λi⁡(j)​(α(j),𝒱)≠∅}\ell=\mathrm{Card}\left\{j\in\{0,\ldots,n_{0}-1\}\ ;\ \Lambda_{i(j)}(\alpha^{(j)},\mathscr{V})\neq\emptyset\right\}, which may a priori depend on the chosen sequence α\alpha.

In order to compute dimℂI∨/tγ−λ​𝒪D~\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I^{\vee}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}, we consider a sequence (α(j))0⩽j⩽n0(\alpha^{(j)})_{0\leqslant j\leqslant n_{0}} with n0=∑i=1p(νi−λi)n_{0}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\nu_{i}-\lambda_{i}\right) satisfying:

  • •

    α(0)=γ−ν\alpha^{(0)}=\gamma-\nu and α(n0)=γ−λ\alpha^{(n_{0})}=\gamma-\lambda

  • •

    for all j∈{0,…​n0−1}j\in\left\{0,\ldots n_{0}-1\right\}, there exists i⁡(j)∈{1,…,p}i(j)\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\} such that α(j+1)=α(j)+ei⁡(j)\alpha^{(j+1)}=\alpha^{(j)}+e_{i(j)}

  • •

    there exists j0∈{0,…,n0−1}j_{0}\in\left\{0,\ldots,n_{0}-1\right\} such that α(j0)=w(0)\alpha^{(j_{0})}=w^{(0)} and α(j0+1)=w(0)+ep\alpha^{(j_{0}+1)}=w^{(0)}+e_{p}

The existence of such a sequence follows from Proposition 2.24. Moreover, this sequence satisfies the required properties of Corollary 2.22.

Let us consider again the plane curve defined by f⁡(x,y)=(x2−y3)​(x4−y3)f(x,y)=(x^{2}-y^{3})(x^{4}-y^{3}) and the ideal I=𝒥DI=\mathscr{J}_{D} of example 2.23. By computing val⁡(𝒪D)\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D}), one can see that the conductor γ\gamma satisfies val⁡(γ)=(8,12)\mathrm{val}(\gamma)=(8,12). The black crosses on figure 3 represent the elements of 𝒱={w∈ℤ2,Δ⁡(γ−v−1¯,I)=∅}\mathscr{V}=\left\{w\in\mathbb{Z}^{2},\Delta(\gamma-v-\underline{1},I)=\emptyset\right\}. Let us assume for example that w(0)=(−2,−4)∉val⁡(I∨)w^{(0)}=(-2,-4)\notin\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}). Then we can for instance consider the sequence α\alpha defined by the grey circles, where α(0)=γ−ν=(−5,−9)\alpha^{(0)}=\gamma-\nu=(-5,-9) and α(n0)=α(13)=γ−λ=(0,−1)\alpha^{(n_{0})}=\alpha^{(13)}=\gamma-\lambda=(0,-1).

Remark 2.25.

In [Pol15] we choose a sort of "canonical" sequence, but it is in fact unnecessary and the presentation here is simpler.

From Corollary 2.22, we have:

(7) dimℂI∨/tγ−λ​𝒪D~=Card⁡{j∈{0,…,n0−1};Λi⁡(j)​(α(j),val⁡(I∨))≠∅}.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I^{\vee}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\mathrm{Card}\left\{j\in\{0,\ldots,n_{0}-1\}\ ;\ \Lambda_{i(j)}(\alpha^{(j)},\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}))\neq\emptyset\right\}.

We want to compare this dimension with the following number ℓ\ell:

(8) ℓ=Card⁡{j∈{0,…,n0−1};Λi⁡(j)​(α(j),𝒱)≠∅}.\ell=\mathrm{Card}\left\{j\in\{0,\ldots,n_{0}-1\}\ ;\ \Lambda_{i(j)}(\alpha^{(j)},\mathscr{V})\neq\emptyset\right\}.
Lemma 2.26.

For the sequence α\alpha defined above, we have:

(9) ℓ⩾1+dimℂI∨/tγ−λ​𝒪D~.\ell\geqslant 1+\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I^{\vee}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}.
Proof.

It is clear that Λi⁡(j)​(α(j),val⁡(I∨))≠∅⇒Λi⁡(j)​(α(j),𝒱)≠∅\Lambda_{i(j)}(\alpha^{(j)},\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}))\neq\emptyset\Rightarrow\Lambda_{i(j)}(\alpha^{(j)},\mathscr{V})\neq\emptyset. Moreover, since there exists j0j_{0} such that α(j0)=w(0)\alpha^{(j_{0})}=w^{(0)} and α(j0+1)=α(j0)+ep\alpha^{(j_{0}+1)}=\alpha^{(j_{0})}+e_{p}, Λp​(α(j0),𝒱)≠∅\Lambda_{p}(\alpha^{(j_{0})},\mathscr{V})\neq\emptyset, but the assumptions on w(0)w^{(0)} implies Λp​(α(j0),val⁡(I∨))=∅\Lambda_{p}(\alpha^{(j_{0})},\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}))=\emptyset. Hence the inequality. ∎

From now on, our sequence α\alpha is fixed.

Third step

The purpose of this third step is to compare this number ℓ\ell to dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}.

For i∈{0,…,n0}i\in\{0,\ldots,n_{0}\} we set β(i)=γ−α(n0−i)\beta^{(i)}=\gamma-\alpha^{(n_{0}-i)}. The sequence β\beta satisfies the properties of Corollary 2.22, so that it can be used to compute the dimension dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}.

We continue with the same example as before. For the sequence α\alpha of Figure 3, we represent the corresponding sequence β\beta on the following diagram. The sequence β\beta is defined for i∈{0,…,13}i\in\left\{0,\ldots,13\right\} by β(i)=γ−α(13−i)\beta^{(i)}=\gamma-\alpha^{(13-i)}. In particular, β(0)=λ\beta^{(0)}=\lambda and β(13)=ν\beta^{(13)}=\nu. The elements of β\beta are represented by grey circles and the elements of II by black crosses. In particular, β(0)=λ=(8,13)\beta^{(0)}=\lambda=(8,13) and β(13)=ν=(13,21)\beta^{(13)}=\nu=(13,21).

The following proposition gives a relation between ℓ\ell and dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}:

Proposition 2.27.

With the above notations we have:

ℓ⩽∑i=1p(νi−λi)−dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~.\ell\leqslant\sum_{i=1}^{p}{(\nu_{i}-\lambda_{i})}-\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}.

To prove this proposition, we need the following lemma:

Lemma 2.28.

Let w∈ℤpw\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} and i∈{1,…,p}i\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\}. Then:

Λi​(w,𝒱)≠∅⇒Λi​(γ−w−ei,val⁡(I))=∅.\Lambda_{i}(w,\mathscr{V})\neq\emptyset\Rightarrow\Lambda_{i}(\gamma-w-e_{i},\mathrm{val}(I))=\emptyset.
Proof.

Let w′∈Λi​(w,𝒱)w^{\prime}\in\Lambda_{i}(w,\mathscr{V}). By the definition of 𝒱\mathscr{V}, we have Δ⁡(γ−w′−1¯,val⁡(I))=∅\Delta(\gamma-w^{\prime}-\underline{1},\mathrm{val}(I))=\emptyset. Moreover, (γ−w′−ei)i=γi−wi−1(\gamma-w^{\prime}-e_{i})_{i}=\gamma_{i}-w_{i}-1 and for j≠ij\neq i, (γ−w′−ei)j=γj−wj′⩽γj−wj(\gamma-w^{\prime}-e_{i})_{j}=\gamma_{j}-w^{\prime}_{j}\leqslant\gamma_{j}-w_{j}. Thus Λi​(γ−w−ei,val⁡(I))=Δi​(γ−w′−1¯,val⁡(I))=∅\Lambda_{i}(\gamma-w-e_{i},\mathrm{val}(I))=\Delta_{i}(\gamma-w^{\prime}-\underline{1},\mathrm{val}(I))=\emptyset, since w′∈𝒱w^{\prime}\in\mathscr{V}. ∎

Proof of Proposition 2.27. We first notice that the two sequences α\alpha and β\beta have the same number of terms, namely n0+1=∑i=1p(νi−λi)+1n_{0}+1=\sum_{i=1}^{p}(\nu_{i}-\lambda_{i})\ +1.

By Corollary 2.22, we have:

(10) dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~=Card​{j∈{0,…,n0−1};Λi⁡(n0−j−1)​(β(j),val⁡(I))≠∅}.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\text{Card}\left\{j\in\{0,\ldots,n_{0}-1\}\ ;\ \Lambda_{i(n_{0}-j-1)}(\beta^{(j)},\mathrm{val}(I))\neq\emptyset\right\}.

We notice that for all j∈{0,…,n0−1}j\in\left\{0,\ldots,n_{0}-1\right\}, γ−α(j)−ei⁡(j)=γ−α(j+1)=β(n0−(j+1))\gamma-\alpha^{(j)}-e_{i(j)}=\gamma-\alpha^{(j+1)}=\beta^{(n_{0}-(j+1))}.

Therefore, by the previous Lemma, if Λi​(α(j),𝒱)≠∅\Lambda_{i}(\alpha^{(j)},\mathscr{V})\neq\emptyset then Λi​(β(n0−(j+1)),val⁡(I))=∅\Lambda_{i}\left(\beta^{(n_{0}-(j+1))},\mathrm{val}(I)\right)=\emptyset. We then obtain the result by comparing (10) and (8). □\Box

2.2.3. End of the proof of Theorem 1.2

We are now able to finish the proof of Theorem 1.2.

We assume now that DD is Gorenstein. The inclusion val⁡(I∨)⊆𝒱\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee})\subseteq\mathscr{V} holds by Proposition 2.18. It remains to prove that this inclusion cannot be strict.

Since ∑i=1p(νi−λi)=dimℂtλ​𝒪D~/tν​𝒪D~=dimℂtλ​𝒪D~/I+dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\nu_{i}-\lambda_{i}\right)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}t^{\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}t^{\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}/I+\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}, we have by Proposition 2.12:

dimℂI∨/tγ−λ​𝒪D~=∑i=1p(νi−λi)−dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I^{\vee}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\nu_{i}-\lambda_{i}\right)\ -\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}.

Thanks to Proposition 2.27, we obtain:

(11) ℓ⩽dimℂI∨/tγ−λ​𝒪D~.\ell\leqslant\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I^{\vee}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}.

However, by Lemma 2.26, if 𝒱≠val⁡(I∨)\mathscr{V}\neq\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}), then ℓ⩾1+dimℂI∨/tγ−λ​𝒪D~\ell\geqslant 1+\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I^{\vee}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}, which contradicts (11). □\Box

Another consequence of the equality 𝒱=val⁡(I∨)\mathscr{V}=\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}) is that the number ℓ\ell is equal to the dimension of I∨/tγ−λ​𝒪D~I^{\vee}/t^{\gamma-\lambda}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}. Therefore, the inequality in Proposition 2.27 is in fact an equality. Moreover, since for all w∈ℤpw\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}, there exist λ′,ν′∈ℤp\lambda^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} such that γ−λ′+ℕp⊆val⁡(I∨)⊆γ−ν′+ℕp\gamma-\lambda^{\prime}+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee})\subseteq\gamma-\nu^{\prime}+\mathbb{N}^{p} and γ−ν′⩽w⩽γ−λ′\gamma-\nu^{\prime}\leqslant w\leqslant\gamma-\lambda^{\prime}, it also has the following consequence:

Corollary 2.29.

Let DD be a Gorenstein curve, I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) be a fractional ideal and w∈ℤpw\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}. Then:

(12) Λi​(w,val⁡(I∨))≠∅⇔Λi​(γ−w−ei,val⁡(I))=∅.\Lambda_{i}(w,\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}))\neq\emptyset\iff\Lambda_{i}(\gamma-w-e_{i},\mathrm{val}(I))=\emptyset.
Corollary 2.30.

Let I,JI,J be fractional ideals and ν∈ℕp\nu\in\mathbb{N}^{p} be such that ν+ℕp⊆J\nu+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq J. We assume val⁡(J)⊆val⁡(I)\mathrm{val}(J)\subseteq\mathrm{val}(I). If dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~=dimℂJ/tν​𝒪D~\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}J/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}} then val⁡(J)=val⁡(I)\mathrm{val}(J)=\mathrm{val}(I).

Proof.

If val⁡(I)≠val⁡(J)\mathrm{val}(I)\neq\mathrm{val}(J), then as in Proposition 2.24, there exists w∈val⁡(I)\val⁡(J)w\in\mathrm{val}(I)\backslash\mathrm{val}(J) and j∈{1,…,p}j\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\} such that Λj​(w,val⁡(J))=∅\Lambda_{j}(w,\mathrm{val}(J))=\emptyset. The same argument as in the second step of the proof of Theorem 1.2 shows that dimℂI/tν​𝒪D~>dimℂJ/tν​𝒪D~\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}>\dim_{\mathbb{C}}J/t^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}. Hence the result. ∎

2.3. Poincaré series of a fractional ideal

This section follows a suggestion of Antonio Campillo. Let (D=D1∪⋯∪Dp,0)(D=D_{1}\cup\dots\cup D_{p},0) be the germ of a reduced reducible Gorenstein curve, and I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) be a fractional ideal.

The following definitions are inspired by [CDGZ03]. We recall that Iv={g∈I;val⁡(g)⩾v}I_{v}=\left\{g\in I;\mathrm{val}(g)\geqslant v\right\}.

We consider the set of formal Laurent series ℒ=ℤ⁡[[t1−1,…,tp−1,t1,…,tp]]\mathscr{L}=\mathbb{Z}[[t_{1}^{-1},\ldots,t_{p}^{-1},t_{1},\ldots,t_{p}]] as in [CDGZ03]. This set is not a ring, it is only a set of formal infinite sums indexed by ℤp\mathbb{Z}^{p}, with a structure of ℤ⁡[t1−1,…,tp−1,t1,…,tp]\mathbb{Z}[t_{1}^{-1},\ldots,t_{p}^{-1},t_{1},\ldots,t_{p}]-module.

We set:

(13) LI​(t1,…,tp)=∑v∈ℤpcI​(v)​tvL_{I}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{p})=\sum_{v\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}}c_{I}(v)t^{v}

with cI​(v)=dimℂIv/Iv+1¯c_{I}(v)=\displaystyle{\dim_{\mathbb{C}}I_{v}/I_{v+\underline{1}}} and

Remark 2.31.

In [CDGZ03], the authors study the case I=𝒪DI=\mathscr{O}_{D} with DD a plane curve. They prove that P𝒪D​(t)P_{\mathscr{O}_{D}}(t) is in fact a polynomial, and for plane curves with at least two components, P𝒪D​(t)t1⋯tp−1\displaystyle{\frac{P_{\mathscr{O}_{D}}(t)}{t_{1}\cdots t_{p}-1}} is the Alexander polynomial of the curve (see [CDGZ03, Theorem 1]).

Our purpose here is to deduce from Theorem 1.2 a relation between PI​(t)P_{I}(t) and PI∨​(t)P_{I^{\vee}}(t).

The following lemma is a direct consequence of the definition of PIP_{I}:

Lemma 2.32.

We define for v∈ℤpv\in\mathbb{Z}^{p},

(15) aI​(v)=∑J⊆{1,…,p}(−1)Card⁡(Jc)​cI​(v−eJ)a_{I}(v)=\sum_{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}}(-1)^{\mathrm{Card}(J^{c})}c_{I}(v-e_{J})

where we denote for J={j1,⋯,jk}J=\{j_{1},\cdots,j_{k}\}, eJ=ej1+⋯+ejke_{J}=e_{j_{1}}+\cdots+e_{j_{k}} and JcJ^{c} the complement of JJ in {1,…,p}\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\}. Then

Lemma 2.33.

The formal Laurent series PI​(t)P_{I}(t) is a polynomial.

Proof.

Let λ,ν∈ℤp\lambda,\nu\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} be such that ν+ℕp⊆val⁡(I)⊆λ+ℕp\nu+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(I)\subseteq\lambda+\mathbb{N}^{p}. The only possibly non-zero aI​(v)a_{I}(v) are those such that λ⩽v⩽ν\lambda\leqslant v\leqslant\nu. Indeed, let us assume for example that vp<λpv_{p}<\lambda_{p} or vp>νpv_{p}>\nu_{p}. We can then prove thanks to Corollary 2.22 that for all J⊂{1,…,p}J\subset\{1,\ldots,p\} such that p∉Jp\notin J, cI​(v−eJ∪{p})=cI​(v−eJ)c_{I}(v-e_{J\cup\{p\}})=c_{I}(v-e_{J}). By definition (15), this gives us the result. ∎

The symmetry of Theorem 1.2 has the following consequence:

Proposition 2.34.

With the same notations,

(16) PI∨​(t)=(−1)p+1​tγ​PI​(1t1,…,1tp).P_{I^{\vee}}(t)=(-1)^{p+1}\ t^{\gamma}\ P_{I}\left(\frac{1}{t_{1}},\ldots,\frac{1}{t_{p}}\right).

(17) ∀v∈ℤp,aI∨​(v)=(−1)p+1​aI​(γ−v).\forall v\in\mathbb{Z}^{p},\ a_{I^{\vee}}(v)=(-1)^{p+1}a_{I}(\gamma-v).

cI∨​(v)=Card⁡{i∈{1,…,p};Λi​(v+e1+⋯+ei−1,val⁡(I∨))≠∅},c_{I^{\vee}}(v)=\mathrm{Card}\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\ ;\ \Lambda_{i}(v+e_{1}+\cdots+e_{i-1},\mathrm{val}(I^{\vee}))\neq\emptyset\},
cI​(γ−v−1)=Card⁡{i∈{1,…,p};Λi​(γ−v−e1−⋯−ei,val⁡(I))≠∅}.c_{I}(\gamma-v-1)=\mathrm{Card}\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\ ;\ \Lambda_{i}(\gamma-v-e_{1}-\cdots-e_{i},\mathrm{val}(I))\neq\emptyset\}.

The result follows from the equivalence (12). ∎

3. On the structure of the set of values of logarithmic residues

In this part we give several properties of the module of logarithmic residues along plane curves or complete intersection curves. We first recall some definitions from [Sai80]. We then focus on the module of logarithmic residues along plane curves. We study the set of its zero divisors and we also give its conductor thanks to Theorem 1.2. We then recall definitions from [AT01] and [Ale12] for complete intersections. We prove that the values of multi-residues are in relation with the values of Kähler differentials.

3.1. Preliminaries on logarithmic residues

We recall here some definitions and results about logarithmic vector fields, logarithmic differential forms and their residues, which can be found in [Sai80]. In this subsection, we consider hypersurfaces, and we will focus on the case of plane curves in subsection 3.2.

Let us consider a reduced hypersurface germ D⊂(ℂn,0)D\subset(\mathbb{C}^{n},0) defined by f∈ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn}f\in\mathbb{C}\left\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right\}. We denote by Θn\Theta_{n} the module of germs of holomorphic vector fields on (ℂn,0)(\mathbb{C}^{n},0) and ℂ⁡{x¯}=ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn}\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}=\mathbb{C}\left\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right\}. We set Ωℂnq\Omega^{q}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}, or Ωq\Omega^{q} for short, the module of holomorphic differential qq-forms.

Definition 3.1.

A germ of vector field δ∈Θn\delta\in\Theta_{n} is called logarithmic along DD if δ⁡(f)=α​f\delta(f)=\alpha f with α∈ℂ​{x¯}\alpha\in\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}. We denote by Der⁡(−log⁡D)\mathrm{Der}(-\log D) the ℂ​{x¯}\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}-module of logarithmic vector fields along DD.

A germ of meromorphic qq-form ω∈1f​Ωq\omega\in\frac{1}{f}\Omega^{q} with simple poles along DD is called logarithmic if f​d​ωf\mathrm{d}\omega is holomorphic. We denote by Ωq​(log⁡D)\Omega^{q}(\log D) the ℂ​{x¯}\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}-module of logarithmic qq-forms on DD.

Lemma 3.2 ([Sai80, Lemma 1.6]).

The two modules Ω1​(log⁡D)\Omega^{1}(\log D) and Der⁡(−log⁡D)\mathrm{Der}(-\log D) are reflexive and each is the dual ℂ​{x¯}\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}-module of the other.

Definition 3.3.

If Der⁡(−log⁡D)\mathrm{Der}(-\log D) (or equivalently Ω1​(log⁡D)\Omega^{1}(\log D)) is a free ℂ​{x¯}\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}-module, we call DD a germ of free divisor.

In particular, plane curves are free divisors (see [Sai80, 1.7]).

Proposition 3.4 (Saito criterion, [Sai80, 1.8]).

The germ DD is free if and only if there exists (δ1,…,δn)(\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{n}) in Der⁡(−log⁡D)\mathrm{Der}(-\log D) such that δj=∑ai​j∂xi\delta_{j}=\sum a_{ij}\partial_{x_{i}} with det((ai​j)1⩽i,j⩽n)=u​f\det\left((a_{ij})_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n}\right)=uf, where uu is invertible in ℂ​{x¯}\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}.

In order to define the notion of logarithmic residues, we need the following characterization of logarithmic differential forms:

Proposition 3.5 ([Sai80, 1.1]).

A meromorphic qq-form ω\omega with simple poles along DD is logarithmic if and only if there exist g∈ℂ​{x¯}g\in\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}, which does not induce a zero divisor in 𝒪D=ℂ​{x¯}/(f)\mathscr{O}_{D}=\mathbb{C}\{\underline{x}\}/(f), a holomorphic (q−1)(q-1)-form ξ\xi and a holomorphic qq-form η\eta such that:

(18) g​ω=d​ff∧ξ+η.g\omega=\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{f}\wedge\xi+\eta.
Definition 3.6.

The residue resq​(ω)\mathrm{res}^{q}(\omega) of ω∈Ωq​(log⁡D)\omega\in\Omega^{q}(\log D) is defined by

resq​(ω):=ξg​ D∈Q⁡(𝒪D)⊗𝒪DΩDq−1,\mathrm{res}^{q}(\omega):=\mathchoice{{\frac{\xi}{g}\,\smash{\vrule height=5.55557pt,depth=1.65279pt}}_{\,D}}{{\frac{\xi}{g}\,\smash{\vrule height=3.88889pt,depth=1.27501pt}}_{\,D}}{{\frac{\xi}{g}\,\smash{\vrule height=2.77777pt,depth=0.85472pt}}_{\,D}}{{\frac{\xi}{g}\,\smash{\vrule height=2.77777pt,depth=1.44028pt}}_{\,D}}\in Q(\mathscr{O}_{D})\otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{D}}\Omega^{q-1}_{D},

where ξ\xi and gg are given by (18), and ΩDq−1=Ωℂnq−1d​f∧Ωℂnq−2+f​Ωℂnq−1​ D\displaystyle{\Omega^{q-1}_{D}=\mathchoice{{\frac{\Omega_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}^{q-1}}{\mathrm{d}f\wedge\Omega_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}^{q-2}+f\Omega^{q-1}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}}\,\smash{\vrule height=6.51204pt,depth=1.65279pt}}_{\,D}}{{\frac{\Omega_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}^{q-1}}{\mathrm{d}f\wedge\Omega_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}^{q-2}+f\Omega^{q-1}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}}\,\smash{\vrule height=4.99203pt,depth=1.27501pt}}_{\,D}}{{\frac{\Omega_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}^{q-1}}{\mathrm{d}f\wedge\Omega_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}^{q-2}+f\Omega^{q-1}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}}\,\smash{\vrule height=3.7861pt,depth=1.59373pt}}_{\,D}}{{\frac{\Omega_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}^{q-1}}{\mathrm{d}f\wedge\Omega_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}^{q-2}+f\Omega^{q-1}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}}\,\smash{\vrule height=3.7861pt,depth=1.59373pt}}_{\,D}}} is the module of Kähler differentials on DD.

If q=1q=1, we write res⁡(ω)\mathrm{res}(\omega) instead of res1​(ω)\mathrm{res}^{1}(\omega).

Definition 3.7.

We define

ℛD:={res⁡(ω);ω∈Ω1​(log⁡D)}⊆Q⁡(𝒪D).\mathscr{R}_{D}:=\left\{\mathrm{res}(\omega);\omega\in\Omega^{1}(\log D)\right\}\subseteq Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}).

We call ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} the module of logarithmic residues of DD.

In particular, ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} is a finite type 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}-module. Moreover, it satisfies the following property:

Lemma 3.8 ([Sai80, Lemma 2.8]).

We have the inclusion 𝒪D~⊆ℛD\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{D}

Notation 3.9.

We denote by 𝒥D⊆𝒪D\mathscr{J}_{D}\subseteq\mathscr{O}_{D} the Jacobian ideal of DD, that is to say the ideal of 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} generated by the partial derivatives of ff.

The following result gives the relation between the module of logarithmic residues and the Jacobian ideal:

Proposition 3.10 ([GS14, Proposition 3.4]).

Let DD be the germ of a reduced divisor. Then 𝒥D∨=ℛD\mathscr{J}_{D}^{\vee}=\mathscr{R}_{D}. If moreover DD is free, ℛD∨=𝒥D\mathscr{R}_{D}^{\vee}=\mathscr{J}_{D}.

3.2. Logarithmic residues along plane curves

We give here several properties of the set of values of logarithmic residues ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} of a plane curve DD. We first determine the zero divisors included in ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}, see Proposition 3.15. We also relate the conductor of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} to the multiplicities of the branches of DD (see Proposition 3.21). We end this subsection with the relation between logarithmic residues and the torsion of Kähler differentials.

Since plane curves are free divisors, the module Ω1​(log⁡D)\Omega^{1}(\log D) is a free ℂ​{x,y}\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}-module of rank 22. Let us assume that ωi=αi​dx+βi​dyf,i=1,2\omega_{i}=\frac{\alpha_{i}\mathrm{d}_{x}+\beta_{i}\mathrm{d}_{y}}{f},\ i=1,2 is a basis of Ω1​(log⁡D)\Omega^{1}(\log D).

If for c1,c2∈ℂc_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{C}, g=c1⋅fx′+c2⋅fy′g=c_{1}\cdot f_{x}^{\prime}+c_{2}\cdot f_{y}^{\prime} induces a non zero divisor in 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}, then the module of residues is generated by res⁡(ω1)=c1⋅α1+c2⋅β1g\displaystyle{\mathrm{res}(\omega_{1})=\frac{c_{1}\cdot\alpha_{1}+c_{2}\cdot\beta_{1}}{g}} and res⁡(ω2)=c1⋅α2+c2⋅β2g\displaystyle{\mathrm{res}(\omega_{2})=\frac{c_{1}\cdot\alpha_{2}+c_{2}\cdot\beta_{2}}{g}}. Thus, the module of logarithmic residues can be generated by two elements.

3.2.1. Zero divisors

Let D=D1∪⋯∪DpD=D_{1}\cup\dots\cup D_{p} be the germ of a reduced plane curve defined by f=f1⋯fpf=f_{1}\cdots f_{p} where for all i∈{1,…,p}i\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\}, fif_{i} is irreducible.

We first want to prove that the negative values of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} determine all the values of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}. It comes from a general property of fractional ideals.

We recall that for g∈Q⁡(𝒪D)g\in Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}), vali​(g)=∞\mathrm{val}_{i}(g)=\infty means that the restriction of gg on DiD_{i} is zero.

The following proposition shows that the values of the zero divisors are determined by the faces of the negative quadrant with origin ν\nu.

Proposition 3.11.

Let I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) be a fractional ideal and let ν∈ℤp\nu\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} be any element satisfying tν​𝒪D~⊆It^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}\subseteq I. Let α∈(ℤ∪{∞})p\alpha\in\left(\mathbb{Z}\cup\left\{\infty\right\}\right)^{p}. Then α∈val⁡(I)¯\alpha\in\overline{\mathrm{val}(I)} if and only if either α∈val⁡(I)\alpha\in\mathrm{val}(I), or the element ww defined by wi=αiw_{i}=\alpha_{i} if αi∈ℕ\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{N} and wi=νiw_{i}=\nu_{i} if αi=∞\alpha_{i}=\infty satisfies w∈val⁡(I)w\in\mathrm{val}(I).

Proof.

Let α∈val⁡(I)¯\alpha\in\overline{\mathrm{val}(I)} be such that α∉val⁡(I)\alpha\notin\mathrm{val}(I). Let α′∈ν+ℕp⊆val⁡(I)\alpha^{\prime}\in\nu+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(I) be such that if αi∈ℕ\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{N}, then αi′⩾αi\alpha_{i}^{\prime}\geqslant\alpha_{i}, and if αi=∞\alpha_{i}=\infty, αi′=νi\alpha_{i}^{\prime}=\nu_{i}. Then, by Proposition 2.9, inf(α,α′)=w∈val⁡(I)\inf(\alpha,\alpha^{\prime})=w\in\mathrm{val}(I) with wi=αiw_{i}=\alpha_{i} if αi∈ℕ\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{N} and wi=νiw_{i}=\nu_{i} if αi=∞\alpha_{i}=\infty.

Conversely, let w∈val⁡(I)w\in\mathrm{val}(I). Let us assume that there exists j∈{1,…,p}j\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\} such that wj=νjw_{j}=\nu_{j}. Let JJ be a set of indices such that for all j∈Jj\in J, wj=νjw_{j}=\nu_{j}. Let us show that the element α\alpha defined by αi=wi\alpha_{i}=w_{i} if i∉Ji\notin J and αi=∞\alpha_{i}=\infty if i∈Ji\in J satisfies α∈val⁡(I)¯\alpha\in\overline{\mathrm{val}(I)}. Let h∈Ih\in I be such that val⁡(h)=w\mathrm{val}(h)=w. Since tν​𝒪D~⊆It^{\nu}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}\subseteq I, there exists g∈Ig\in I such that for all j∈Jj\in J, g|Dj=h|Djg|_{D_{j}}=h|_{D_{j}} and for all j∉Jj\notin J, valj​(g)>wj\mathrm{val}_{j}(g)>w_{j}. Then h−gh-g is a zero divisor of II whose value α\alpha satisfies for all j∈Jj\in J, αj=∞\alpha_{j}=\infty and for all j∉Jj\notin J, αj=wj\alpha_{j}=w_{j}. ∎

We will use the notation ℳI={w∈val⁡(I);Card⁡{j∈{1,…,p};wj=νj}⩾1}\mathscr{M}_{I}=\left\{w\in\mathrm{val}(I)\ ;\ \mathrm{Card}\left\{j\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\}\ ;\ w_{j}=\nu_{j}\right\}\geqslant 1\right\}. This set determines the value of the zero divisors of Q⁡(𝒪D)Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}).

Corollary 3.12.

Let I⊂Q⁡(𝒪D)I\subset Q(\mathscr{O}_{D}) be a fractional ideal and ν∈ℤp\nu\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} be such that ν+ℕp⊆val⁡(I)\nu+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(I). Let w∈ℤpw\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}. Then

w∈val⁡(I)⇔inf(w,ν)∈val⁡(I).w\in\mathrm{val}(I)\iff\inf(w,\nu)\in\mathrm{val}(I).

In particular, it means that the set

val⁡(I)∩{w∈ℤp;w⩽ν}\mathrm{val}(I)\cap\left\{w\in\mathbb{Z}^{p};w\leqslant\nu\right\}

determines the set val⁡(I)\mathrm{val}(I).

Proof.

The implication ⇒\Rightarrow comes from Proposition 2.9. For the implication ⇐\Leftarrow, let w∈ℤpw\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} be such that inf(w,ν)∈val⁡(I)\inf(w,\nu)\in\mathrm{val}(I). If w⩽νw\leqslant\nu, then w=inf(w,ν)∈val⁡(I)w=\inf(w,\nu)\in\mathrm{val}(I). If there exists jj such that wj>νjw_{j}>\nu_{j}, then inf(w,ν)∈ℳI\inf(w,\nu)\in\mathscr{M}_{I} where ℳI\mathscr{M}_{I} is defined after Proposition 3.11. By Proposition 3.11, there exist a zero divisor g∈Ig\in I such that valj​(g)=∞\mathrm{val}_{j}(g)=\infty if wj⩾νjw_{j}\geqslant\nu_{j} and valj​(g)=wj\mathrm{val}_{j}(g)=w_{j} if wj<νjw_{j}<\nu_{j}. Let v=max⁡(w,ν)v=\max(w,\nu). Since ν+ℕp⊆val⁡(I)\nu+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(I), we have v∈val⁡(I)v\in\mathrm{val}(I) and w=inf(v,val⁡(g))∈val⁡(I)w=\inf(v,\mathrm{val}(g))\in\mathrm{val}(I). ∎

Remark 3.13.

By Proposition 3.11 and Corollary 3.12, the set val⁡(I)∩{w∈ℤp;w⩽ν}\mathrm{val}(I)\cap\left\{w\in\mathbb{Z}^{p};w\leqslant\nu\right\} also determines val⁡(I)¯\overline{\mathrm{val}(I)}.

The inclusion 𝒪D~⊆ℛD\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{D} gives the following corollary:

Corollary 3.14.

The set of values of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} is determined by the set

{v∈val⁡(ℛD);v⩽0}.\left\{v\in\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{R}_{D});v\leqslant 0\right\}.

More precisely, we have:

val(ℛD)={v∈val(ℛD);v⩽0}∪{v∈ℤp;inf(v,0)∈val(ℛD)}.\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{R}_{D})=\left\{v\in\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{R}_{D});v\leqslant 0\right\}\cup\left\{v\in\mathbb{Z}^{p};\inf(v,0)\in\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{R}_{D})\right\}.

Let us determine the values of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} which come from the branches or union of branches.

Proposition 3.15.

Let ∅≠J⊆{1,…,p}\emptyset\neq J\subseteq\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\} and D′=⋃j∈JDjD^{\prime}=\bigcup_{j\in J}D_{j}. Then Ω1​(log⁡D′)⊆Ω1​(log⁡D)\Omega^{1}(\log D^{\prime})\subseteq\Omega^{1}(\log D).

Renumbering the branches, we may assume that J={1,…,q}J=\left\{1,\ldots,q\right\} with q⩽pq\leqslant p. Then:

ℛD∩(Q⁡(𝒪D1)⊕⋯⊕Q⁡(𝒪Dq)⊕{0}p−q)=ℛD′.\mathscr{R}_{D}\cap\left(Q(\mathscr{O}_{D_{1}})\oplus\dots\oplus Q(\mathscr{O}_{D_{q}})\oplus\left\{0\right\}^{p-q}\right)=\mathscr{R}_{D^{\prime}}.
Proof.

For the first part of the statement, we set F1F_{1} the equation of D′D^{\prime}. Let ω\omega be a logarithmic 11-form along D′D^{\prime}. Then, F1​ωF_{1}\omega and F1​d​ωF_{1}\mathrm{d}\omega are holomorphic, so that f​ωf\omega and f​d​ωf\mathrm{d}\omega are holomorphic.

For the second part of the statement, let us notice the following property. Let ω∈Ω1​(log⁡D)\omega\in\Omega^{1}(\log D). Then ω∈Ω1​(log⁡D′)\omega\in\Omega^{1}(\log D^{\prime}) if and only if for all j∉Jj\notin J, valj​(res​(ω))=∞\mathrm{val}_{j}(\mathrm{res}(\omega))=\infty. The second part of the statement then follows from this remark and Proposition 3.11. ∎

In particular, the logarithmic residues of the irreducible components satisfy the following property:

Corollary 3.16.

We have the following inclusion:

ℛD1⊕⋯⊕ℛDp↪ℛD.\mathscr{R}_{D_{1}}\oplus\dots\oplus\mathscr{R}_{D_{p}}\hookrightarrow\mathscr{R}_{D}.

Therefore, val1​(ℛD1)×⋯×valp​(ℛDp)⊆val⁡(ℛD)\mathrm{val}_{1}(\mathscr{R}_{D_{1}})\times\dots\times\mathrm{val}_{p}(\mathscr{R}_{D_{p}})\subseteq\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{R}_{D}).

Remark 3.17.

If D=D1∪D2D=D_{1}\cup D_{2} is a plane curve satisfying ℛD=ℛD1⊕ℛD2\mathscr{R}_{D}=\mathscr{R}_{D_{1}}\oplus\mathscr{R}_{D_{2}}, then by [Sch16], it is a splayed divisor, and in fact it is even a normal crossing plane curve. We refer to [Fab13, Definition 2.3] for the definition of a splayed divisor.

We now study the set of values of the dual of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}, namely, the Jacobian ideal 𝒥D\mathscr{J}_{D}. We show that the modules of logarithmic vector fields Der⁡(−log⁡Di)\mathrm{Der}(-\log D_{i}) for i∈{1,…,p}i\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\} give information on the structure of the set of values of the Jacobian ideal.

Proposition 3.18.

Let ∅≠J⊆{1,…,p}\emptyset\neq J\subseteq\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\} and D′=⋃j∈JDjD^{\prime}=\bigcup_{j\in J}D_{j}. Renumbering the branches, we may assume that J={1,…,q}J=\left\{1,\ldots,q\right\} with q⩽pq\leqslant p. Then:

𝒥D∩({0}q⊕ℂ⁡{tq+1}⊕⋯⊕ℂ⁡{tp})={δ⁡(h);δ∈Der⁡(−log⁡D′)}.\mathscr{J}_{D}\cap\left(\left\{0\right\}^{q}\oplus\mathbb{C}\left\{t_{q+1}\right\}\oplus\dots\oplus\mathbb{C}\left\{t_{p}\right\}\right)=\left\{\delta(h)\ ;\ \delta\in\mathrm{Der}(-\log D^{\prime})\right\}.

{Der(−log(∪j∈JDj))}J⊂{1,…,p},J≠∅.\left\{\mathrm{Der}\big(-\log(\cup_{j\in J}D_{j})\big)\right\}_{J\subset\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\},J\neq\emptyset}.

Moreover, δ⁡(f)\delta(f) induces in 𝒪D~=∏i=1p𝒪Di~\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D_{i}}} the element:

δ(f)=(f2⋯fpδ(f1),…,f1⋯fp−1δ(fp)).\delta(f)=\left(f_{2}\cdots f_{p}\delta(f_{1}),\ldots,f_{1}\cdots f_{p-1}\delta(f_{p})\right).

By Proposition 3.11, v∈ℳ𝒥Dv\in\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{J}_{D}} if and only if there are ∅≠J⊆{1,…,p}\emptyset\neq J\subseteq\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\} and δ∈Θ2\delta\in\Theta_{2} such that for all j∈Jj\in J, valj​(δ​(f))=∞\mathrm{val}_{j}(\delta(f))=\infty and for all j∉Jj\notin J, valj​(δ⁡(f))=vj\mathrm{val}_{j}(\delta(f))=v_{j}. 3.2.2. Conductor of the module of residues

We compute here the conductor of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}, that is to say, the minimal ν∈ℤp\nu\in\mathbb{Z}^{p} such that ν+ℕp⊆val⁡(ℛD)\nu+\mathbb{N}^{p}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{R}_{D}).

We need the following results:

Proposition 3.19 ([DdlM87, Theorem 2.7]).

Let f=f1⋯fpf=f_{1}\cdots f_{p} be a reduced equation of a plane curve germ. We assume that for all i∈{1,…,p}i\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\}, fif_{i} is irreducible. We denote by cic_{i} the conductor of the branch defined by fif_{i}. The conductor of DD is given by

γ=(c1+∑i=2pval1​(fi),…,cp+∑i=1p−1valp​(fi)).\gamma=\left(c_{1}+\sum_{i=2}^{p}{\mathrm{val}_{1}(f_{i})},\ldots,c_{p}+\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}{\mathrm{val}_{p}(f_{i})}\right).

We then have:

Lemma 3.20.

Let f∈ℂ​{x,y}f\in\mathbb{C}\{x,y\} be a reduced equation of a plane curve germ. Then:

val⁡(fx′)\displaystyle\mathrm{val}(f_{x}^{\prime}) =γ+val⁡(y)−1¯\displaystyle=\gamma+\mathrm{val}(y)-\underline{1}
val⁡(fy′)\displaystyle\mathrm{val}(f_{y}^{\prime}) =γ+val⁡(x)−1¯\displaystyle=\gamma+\mathrm{val}(x)-\underline{1}
Proof.

If ff is irreducible, it is exactly the statement of Teissier’s lemma (see [CNP11, Lemma 2.3]). If ff is reducible, we prove the result for fx′f_{x}^{\prime}. We have the following equality:

valj​(fx′)=∑i≠jvalj​(fi)+valj​(∂fj∂x).\mathrm{val}_{j}\left(f_{x}^{\prime}\right)=\sum_{i\neq j}\mathrm{val}_{j}(f_{i})+\mathrm{val}_{j}\left(\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x}\right).

The conductor of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} is −(m(1),…,m(p))+1¯-(m^{(1)},\ldots,m^{(p)})+\underline{1}, where m(j)=inf(valj​(x),valj​(y))m^{(j)}=\inf(\mathrm{val}_{j}(x),\mathrm{val}_{j}(y)) is the multiplicity of the component DjD_{j} of DD.

sup{α∈ℤp;∀β⩽α,Δ(β,𝒥D)=∅}=γ+inf(val(x),val(y))−2¯.\sup\left\{\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}\ ;\forall\beta\leqslant\alpha,\Delta(\beta,\mathscr{J}_{D})=\emptyset\right\}=\gamma+\inf(\mathrm{val}(x),\mathrm{val}(y))-\underline{2}.

Therefore, resq​(Ωq​(log⁡D))≃Ωq​(log⁡D)Ωℂnq\mathrm{res}^{q}(\Omega^{q}(\log D))\simeq\frac{\Omega^{q}(\log D)}{\Omega^{q}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}} and ΩDq−1≃d​ff∧Ωq−1​ℂn+ΩℂnqΩℂnq\Omega^{q-1}_{D}\simeq\frac{\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{f}\wedge\Omega^{q-1}{\mathbb{C}^{n}}+\Omega^{q}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}}{\Omega^{q}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}}, so that by a classical isomorphism theorem, we have resq​(Ωq​(log⁡D))ΩDq−1≃Ωq​(log⁡D)d​ff∧Ωℂnq−1+Ωℂnq\frac{\mathrm{res}^{q}(\Omega^{q}(\log D))}{\Omega^{q-1}_{D}}\simeq\frac{\Omega^{q}(\log D)}{\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{f}\wedge\Omega^{q-1}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}+\Omega^{q}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}}, and we conclude with Proposition 3.22. ∎

Let D⊆(ℂ2,0)D\subseteq(\mathbb{C}^{2},0) be a plane curve germ. We denote by τ=dimC𝒪D/𝒥D\tau=\dim_{C}\mathscr{O}_{D}/\mathscr{J}_{D} the Tjurina number. This section is devoted to the study of complete intersection curves, which are a particular case of Gorenstein curves.

We begin with the definition of multi-logarithmic forms along a reduced complete intersection given in [Ale12]. We then focus on the case of complete intersection curves for which we give the relation between the values of multi-residues and the values of Kähler differentials.

The latter corollary gives also the relation between meromorphic regular forms as defined in [Bar78] and Kähler differentials. Indeed, by [AT01, Théorème 2.4], the module ℛC\mathscr{R}_{C} of multi-residues is isomorphic to the module of regular meromorphic forms ωC\omega_{C}, which can be defined as ωC=Ext𝒪ℂmm−1​(𝒪C,Ωℂmm)\omega_{C}=\mathrm{Ext}^{m-1}_{\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}}\left(\mathscr{O}_{C},\Omega^{m}_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}\right). In particular, ωC≃1g⋅(φ∗​(ΩC1)d​t¯)∨\displaystyle{\omega_{C}\simeq\frac{1}{g}\cdot\left(\frac{\varphi^{*}(\Omega^{1}_{C})}{\underline{\mathrm{d}t}}\right)^{\vee}}.

Remark 3.34.

Another consequence of Proposition 3.31 is the following inclusion:

γ+(val⁡(𝒪C)\{0¯})−1¯⊆val⁡(𝒥C).\gamma+\big(\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{C})\backslash\{\underline{0}\}\big)-\underline{1}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{J}_{C}).

Indeed, if h∈𝔪h\in\mathfrak{m}, with 𝔪\mathfrak{m} the maximal ideal of 𝒪C\mathscr{O}_{C}, then val⁡(d​h)=val⁡(h)\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{d}h)=\mathrm{val}(h), which gives us the inclusion val⁡(𝒪C)\{0}⊆val⁡(ΩC1)\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{C})\backslash\left\{0\right\}\subseteq\mathrm{val}(\Omega^{1}_{C}).

4. Equisingular deformations of plane curves and the stratification by logarithmic residues

The purpose of this last section is to study the behaviour of the values of logarithmic residues in an equisingular deformation of a plane curve. The base space of this deformation is denoted by SS in forthcoming definition 4.5. Each s∈Ss\in S is associated with a germ of plane curve DsD_{s}, and val⁡(𝒪Ds)\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D_{s}}) does not depend on ss. By the results of section 3, partitioning SS by the values of logarithmic residues is the same as by the values of Kähler differentials. This partition is an essential ingredient of the analytic classification of plane curves described in [HH11] and [HHH15] respectively for irreducible curves and for reducible curves with two branches.

We first recall some results on equisingular and admissible deformations. We then prove that the stratification by the values of logarithmic residues is finite and constructible, and it refines the stratification by the Tjurina number (see Propositions 4.14 and 4.15). We end this section with several algorithms which can be used to compute the set of values of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}, inspired by [BGM88] and [HH07].

Definition 4.1 ([dJP00, Definition 10.1.1]).

Let DD be a plane curve defined in a neighbourhood UU of the origin of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} by a reduced equation f∈𝒪ℂ2​(U)f\in\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}(U). Let k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and (S,0)=(ℂk,0)(S,0)=(\mathbb{C}^{k},0). A deformation FF of ff with base space SS is a function F⁡(x,y,s)∈𝒪ℂ2​⊗^​𝒪SF(x,y,s)\in\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}\widehat{\otimes}\mathscr{O}_{S} which satisfies F⁡(x,y,0)=f⁡(x,y)F(x,y,0)=f(x,y).

For the remainder of this section, we set:

Notation 4.2.

Let X=U×SX=U\times S, 𝒪X=𝒪ℂ2​⊗^​𝒪S\mathscr{O}_{X}=\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}\widehat{\otimes}\mathscr{O}_{S}, W=F−1​(0)⊆U×SW=F^{-1}(0)\subseteq U\times S. We assume F⁡(0,0,s)=0F(0,0,s)=0 for all ss. For s∈Ss\in S, we set Ds=W∩(ℂ2×{s})D_{s}=W\cap\left(\mathbb{C}^{2}\times\{s\}\right) and 𝔪S,s\mathfrak{m}_{S,s} the maximal ideal of 𝒪S,s\mathscr{O}_{S,s}, and Fs=F(.,s)F_{s}=F(.,s). In particular, D0=DD_{0}=D and F0=fF_{0}=f.

4.1. Equisingular and admissible deformations of plane curves

The following numbers are classical invariants of plane curves:

Definition 4.3.

Let DD be a reduced plane curve defined by f∈ℂ​{x,y}f\in\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}.

  • •

    The Milnor number of ff is μ⁡(f)=dimℂℂ⁡{x,y}/(fx′,fy′)\mu(f)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}/(f_{x}^{\prime},f_{y}^{\prime})

  • •

    The Tjurina number of ff is τ⁡(f)=dimℂℂ⁡{x,y}/(fx′,fy′,f)\tau(f)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}/(f_{x}^{\prime},f_{y}^{\prime},f)

  • •

    The delta-invariant of ff is δ⁡(f)=dimℂ𝒪D~/𝒪D\delta(f)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}/\mathscr{O}_{D}

The following proposition gives the relation between μ\mu and δ\delta:

Proposition 4.4 ([Mil68]).

We have the following relation:

μ⁡(f)=2⋅δ⁡(f)−p+1,\mu(f)=2\cdot\delta(f)-p+1,

where pp is the number of irreducible components of DD.

Definition 4.5.

Let FF be a deformation of ff with base space SS. We say that FF is an equisingular deformation of ff if for all s∈Ss\in S, μ⁡(Fs)=μ⁡(f)\mu(F_{s})=\mu(f).

From the equisingularity Theorem for plane curves (see [Tei77, §3.7]), for an equisingular deformation of a plane curve, a parametrization φ\varphi of DD gives rise to a deformation φs\varphi_{s} of the parametrization. We denote by valDs​(g)\mathrm{val}_{D_{s}}(g) the value of g∈Q⁡(𝒪Ds)g\in Q(\mathscr{O}_{D_{s}}) along DsD_{s}. Another consequence of the equisingularity Theorem for plane curves is:

Corollary 4.6.

With the same notations, if FF is an equisingular deformation of ff:

  1. (1)

    All fibers DsD_{s} have the same conductor γ\gamma.

  2. (2)

    Let x⁡(t,s)=(x1​(t1,s),…,xp​(tp,s)),y⁡(t,s)=(y1​(t1,s),…,yp​(tp,s))x(t,s)=(x_{1}(t_{1},s),\ldots,x_{p}(t_{p},s)),y(t,s)=(y_{1}(t_{1},s),\ldots,y_{p}(t_{p},s)) be a parametrization of DsD_{s}. For all s∈Ss\in S,

    inf(valDs​(x⁡(t,s)),valDs​(y⁡(t,s)))=inf(valD​(x⁡(t,0)),valD​(y⁡(t,0)))=(m(1),…,m(p)),\inf\big(\mathrm{val}_{D_{s}}(x(t,s)),\mathrm{val}_{D_{s}}(y(t,s))\big)=\inf\big(\mathrm{val}_{D}(x(t,0)),\mathrm{val}_{D}(y(t,0))\big)=(m^{(1)},\ldots,m^{(p)}),

    where m(j)m^{(j)} is the multiplicity of the component DjD_{j} of DD.

Proof.

  1. (1)

    By the equisingularity Theorem (see [Tei77, §3.7, (10)]), the intersection multiplicity of any couple of branches, and the characteristic exponents of each branch, do not depend on ss. Thus, the semigroup and therefore the conductor of each branch are also independent from ss. Theorem 3.19 then gives the result.

  2. (2)

    For all j∈{1,…,p}j\in\left\{1,\ldots,p\right\}, inf(valDs,j​(xj​(tj,s)),valDs,j​(yj​(tj,s)))\inf\big(\mathrm{val}_{D_{s,j}}(x_{j}(t_{j},s)),\mathrm{val}_{D_{s,j}}(y_{j}(t_{j},s))\big) is the multiplicity of Ds,jD_{s,j}, which does not depend on ss by the equisingularity Theorem.

∎

The following proposition will be used in the next subsection, since it gives a common denominator for the logarithmic residues with interesting properties.

Proposition 4.7.

There exists α,β∈ℂ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C} such that for all ss in a neighbourhood of 00, val⁡(α​Fx′​(s)+β​Fy′​(s))=γ+(m(1),…,m(p))−1¯\mathrm{val}(\alpha F_{x}^{\prime}(s)+\beta F_{y}^{\prime}(s))=\gamma+\left(m^{(1)},\ldots,m^{(p)}\right)-\underline{1}. In particular, α​Fx′​(s)+β​Fy′​(s)\alpha F_{x}^{\prime}(s)+\beta F_{y}^{\prime}(s) induces a non zero divisor in 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} whose value does not depend on ss.

Proof.

Thanks to the equisingularity Theorem, one can prove that there exists a linear change of coordinates (u,v)(u,v) such that for all ss in a neighbourhood of 0∈S0\in S, valDs​(u)=(m(1),…,m(p))\mathrm{val}_{D_{s}}(u)=\left(m^{(1)},\ldots,m^{(p)}\right). The conclusion follows from Corollary 4.6 and Lemma 3.20. ∎

We want now to understand the behaviour of a generating family of the module of residues.

We recall that plane curves are free divisors. Moreover, they are the only free divisors with isolated singularities, since by [Ale88], the singular locus of a free divisor is of codimension one in the hypersurface. The equisingularity assumption is not sufficient to obtain a deformation (ρ1​(s),ρ2​(s))(\rho_{1}(s),\rho_{2}(s)) of a generating family of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} such that (ρ1​(s),ρ2​(s))(\rho_{1}(s),\rho_{2}(s)) generate ℛDs\mathscr{R}_{D_{s}}: equisingularity is not the "good" functor of deformation for free divisors. A functor of deformation adapted to free divisors is suggested by M.Torielli in [Tor13].

The following definition is equivalent to the definition of M.Torielli (see [Tor13, Definition 3.1]) thanks to both [Tor13, Proposition 3.7] and [GLS07, Theorem 1.91]:

Definition 4.8.

Let DD be a free divisor defined in a neighbourhood of 0∈ℂn0\in\mathbb{C}^{n} by a reduced equation ff. An admissible deformation XX of DD with base space SS is a deformation of DD such that the module 𝒪ℂn×S,0/(F,Fx′,Fy′)\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}\times S,0}/(F,F_{x}^{\prime},F_{y}^{\prime}) is a flat 𝒪S,0\mathscr{O}_{S,0}-module.

The following proposition describes an admissible deformation of a plane curve thanks to the Tjurina number.

Proposition 4.9.

Let FF be a deformation of f∈𝒪ℂ2​(U)f\in\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}(U) with base space SS such that for all s∈Ss\in S, ∑xj∈S​i​n​g​(Ds)τxj=τ0\sum_{x_{j}\in Sing(D_{s})}\tau_{x_{j}}=\tau_{0} where τ0\tau_{0} is the Tjurina number of D0D_{0}. Such a deformation is an admissible deformation.

Proof.

We denote by pp the restriction of the canonical epimorphism ℂ2×S→S\mathbb{C}^{2}\times S\to S to the relative singular locus, which is a finite morphism. We set ℱ=p∗​(𝒪ℂ2×S/(F,∂F∂x,∂F∂y))\mathscr{F}=p_{*}\left(\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}\times S}/\left(F,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x},\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}\right)\right). Then ℱs/𝔪S,s​ℱs=𝒪ℂ2/(Fs,∂Fs∂x,∂Fs∂y)\mathscr{F}_{s}/\mathfrak{m}_{S,s}\mathscr{F}_{s}=\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}/\left(F_{s},\frac{\partial F_{s}}{\partial x},\frac{\partial F_{s}}{\partial y}\right), which is by assumption a complex vector space of dimension τ0\tau_{0}. The proposition is then a direct consequence of [GLS07, Theorem 1.81]. ∎

Let F⁡(x,y,s)F(x,y,s) be an equisingular and admissible deformation of the plane curve defined by ff with base space SS. Let (δ1,δ2)(\delta_{1},\delta_{2}) be a basis of the module of logarithmic vector fields along DD. Then δ1,δ2\delta_{1},\delta_{2} induce relations between f,fx′,fy′f,f_{x}^{\prime},f_{y}^{\prime}. By flatness, we can extend them to obtain relative logarithmic vector fields δ~1,δ~2∈(ΘU×S/S)/(𝔪S​ΘU×S/S)\widetilde{\delta}_{1},\widetilde{\delta}_{2}\in(\Theta_{U\times S/S})/(\mathfrak{m}_{S}\Theta_{U\times S/S}) of FF. Then, for ss in a neighbourhood of 0∈S0\in S, (δ~1​(s),δ~2​(s))\left(\widetilde{\delta}_{1}(s),\widetilde{\delta}_{2}(s)\right) is a basis of Der⁡(−log⁡Ds)\mathrm{Der}(-\log D_{s}).

Let δ~i=Ai(s)∂x+Bi(s)∂y\widetilde{\delta}_{i}=A_{i}(s)\partial_{x}+B_{i}(s)\partial_{y}, i=1,2i=1,2 be as in Proposition 4.10. Thanks to the duality between the modules Der⁡(−log⁡Ds)\mathrm{Der}(-\log D_{s}) and Ω1​(log⁡Ds)\Omega^{1}(\log D_{s}), the following elements generate the module of residues for all ss in a neighbourhood of 0∈S0\in S:

{ρ1​(s)=−β​A2​(s)+α​B2​(s)α​Fx′​(s)+β​Fy′​(s)ρ2​(s)=β​A1​(s)−α​B1​(s)α​Fx′​(s)+β​Fy′​(s)\left\{\begin{aligned} \rho_{1}(s)&=\frac{-\beta A_{2}(s)+\alpha B_{2}(s)}{\alpha F_{x}^{\prime}(s)+\beta F_{y}^{\prime}(s)}\\ \rho_{2}(s)&=\frac{\beta A_{1}(s)-\alpha B_{1}(s)}{\alpha F_{x}^{\prime}(s)+\beta F_{y}^{\prime}(s)}\end{aligned}\right.

where α,β∈ℂ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C} are given by Proposition 4.7.

4.2. Properties of the stratification by logarithmic residues

We consider an equisingular deformation FF of ff with base space (S,0)≃(ℂk,0)(S,0)\simeq(\mathbb{C}^{k},0) for a k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. We denote by ℛs\mathscr{R}_{s} the module of logarithmic residues of DsD_{s}.

The purpose of this section is to study the stratification by the values of logarithmic residues defined in Definition 4.12. We prove that this stratification is finite, finer than the stratification by the Tjurina number and constructible (see Propositions 4.14 and 4.15). We end with two examples, the first one shows that the stratification by logarithmic residues may be strictly finer than the stratification by the Tjurina number (see Example 4.16). The stratification by logarithmic residues of Example 4.19 does not satisfy the frontier condition.

Definition 4.12.

Let F⁡(x,y,s)F(x,y,s) be an equisingular deformation of a reduced plane curve DD with pp branches defined by f∈ℂ​{x,y}f\in\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}, with base space SS. The stratification by logarithmic residues is the partition S=⋃𝒱⊆ℤpS𝒱S=\bigcup_{\mathscr{V}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{p}}S_{\mathscr{V}} where s∈S𝒱s\in S_{\mathscr{V}} if and only if val⁡(ℛs)=𝒱\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{R}_{s})=\mathscr{V}.

An example of a stratification by the values of logarithmic residues is given in example 4.16.

Let us compare the stratification by logarithmic residues with the stratification by the Tjurina number. The stratification by the Tjurina number is the partition S=⋃n∈ℕSnS=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}S_{n} where s∈Sns\in S_{n} if and only if τ⁡(Fs)=n\tau(F_{s})=n. This stratification is finite since the Tjurina number is bounded by the Milnor number, which is constant on SS by the equisingularity condition.

Proposition 4.13.

Let DD be a plane curve germ. Then:

(22) dimℂℛD/𝒪D~=τ−δ.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{R}_{D}/\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\tau-\delta.
Proof.

Thanks to Propositions 2.12 and 3.10 we have:

dimℂℛD/𝒪D~\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{R}_{D}/\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}} =dimℂℛD/𝒪D−dimℂ𝒪D~/𝒪D=dimℂ𝒪D∨/ℛD∨−δ=dimℂ𝒪D/𝒥D−δ\displaystyle=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{R}_{D}/\mathscr{O}_{D}-\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}/\mathscr{O}_{D}=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{O}_{D}^{\vee}/\mathscr{R}_{D}^{\vee}-\delta=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{O}_{D}/\mathscr{J}_{D}-\delta
=τ−δ\displaystyle=\tau-\delta

∎

Proposition 4.14.

The stratification by logarithmic residues satisfies the following properties:

  1. (1)

    The stratification by logarithmic residues is finer than the stratification by the Tjurina number.

  2. (2)

    The stratification by logarithmic residues is finite.

Proof.

The first claim is a direct consequence of Proposition 4.13, since the equisingularity condition ensures that δ⁡(Fs)\delta(F_{s}) does not depend on ss, and the dimension of the quotient ℛs/𝒪Ds~\mathscr{R}_{s}/\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D_{s}}} can be computed from the values of ℛs\mathscr{R}_{s} by Corollary 2.22. The second claim comes from both Proposition 4.7, which gives a lower bound uu of the set of values of logarithmic residues which do not depend on ss, and Corollary 3.14. As a consequence, the values of ℛs\mathscr{R}_{s} are determined by the values vv of ℛs\mathscr{R}_{s} satisfying u⩽v⩽0u\leqslant v\leqslant 0. ∎

Proposition 4.15.

Each stratum S𝒱S_{\mathscr{V}} of the stratification by logarithmic residues is constructible. If moreover DD is irreducible, then each stratum is locally closed.

The hypothesis of DD being irreducible was forgotten in the corresponding statement [Pol15, Proposition 4.2].

Proof.

By the appendix by Teissier in [Zar86], the strata of the stratification by the Tjurina number are locally analytic and locally closed. It is therefore sufficient to consider the behaviour of logarithmic residues in a τ\tau-constant stratum SτS_{\tau}. For the sake of simplicity, we denote S=SτS=S_{\tau}.

By Corollary 4.11, for all ss, the 𝒪S\mathscr{O}_{S}-module ℛs\mathscr{R}_{s} is generated by

We recall here the examples of [Pol15] with more details. The first example shows that the stratification by logarithmic residues may be strictly finer than the stratification by the Tjurina number, whereas the second shows that the stratification by logarithmic residues does not satisfy the frontier condition defined below.

Example 4.16.
