Example 4.19 below shows that the stratification by logarithmic residues do not necessarily satisfy the frontier condition defined below.

Definition 4.17.

A stratification S=⋃αSαS=\bigcup_{\alpha}S_{\alpha} satisfies the frontier condition if for α≠β\alpha\neq\beta, Sα∩Sβ¯≠∅S_{\alpha}\cap\overline{S_{\beta}}\neq\emptyset implies Sα⊆Sβ¯S_{\alpha}\subseteq\overline{S_{\beta}}, with Sβ¯\overline{S_{\beta}} the closure of SβS_{\beta}.

We first prove the following property:

Lemma 4.18.

Let DD be a quasi-homogeneous plane curve germ with conductor γ\gamma. Then:

γ−1¯+(val⁡(𝒪D)\{0})=val⁡(𝒥D).\gamma-\underline{1}+\left(\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D})\backslash\{0\}\right)=\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{J}_{D}).
Proof.

Let pp be the number of branches. The inclusion ⊆\subseteq is given by Remark 3.34. For the other inclusion, we notice that Remark 3.34 implies t2​γ−1¯​𝒪D~⊆𝒥D⊆𝒞Dt^{2\gamma-\underline{1}}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}\subseteq\mathscr{J}_{D}\subseteq\mathscr{C}_{D}. We have the following equality:

dimℂ𝒞D/t2​γ−1​𝒪D~=dimℂ𝒞D/𝒥D+dimℂ𝒥D/t2​γ−1¯​𝒪D~.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{C}_{D}/t^{2\gamma-1}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{C}_{D}/\mathscr{J}_{D}+\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{J}_{D}/t^{2\gamma-\underline{1}}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}.

By Propositions 4.13 and 2.12, we have dimℂ𝒞D/𝒥D=τ−δ\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{C}_{D}/\mathscr{J}_{D}=\tau-\delta. Since DD is quasi-homogeneous, we have τ=μ\tau=\mu so that by Proposition 4.4 we have dimℂ𝒞D/𝒥D=δ−p+1\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{C}_{D}/\mathscr{J}_{D}=\delta-p+1. Moreover, since δ=dimℂ𝒪D~/𝒪D\delta=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}/\mathscr{O}_{D}, and since CC is Gorenstein, dimℂ𝒪D/𝒞D=δ\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{O}_{D}/\mathscr{C}_{D}=\delta, we have dimℂ𝒪D~/𝒞D=2​δ\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}/\mathscr{C}_{D}=2\delta, thus dimℂ𝒞D/t2​γ−1​𝒪D~=2​δ−p\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{C}_{D}/t^{2\gamma-1}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=2\delta-p. Therefore:

dimℂ𝒥D/t2​γ−1​𝒪D~=δ−1.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathscr{J}_{D}/t^{2\gamma-1}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\delta-1.

Let 𝔪\mathfrak{m} be the maximal ideal of 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D}. Then val⁡(𝔪)=val⁡(𝒪D)\{0}\mathrm{val}(\mathfrak{m})=\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D})\backslash\{0\} and the quotient 𝔪/𝒞D\mathfrak{m}/\mathscr{C}_{D} has dimension δ−1\delta-1. Therefore, dimℂtγ−1¯​𝔪/t2​γ−1¯​𝒪D~=δ−1\dim_{\mathbb{C}}t^{\gamma-\underline{1}}\mathfrak{m}/t^{2\gamma-\underline{1}}\mathscr{O}_{\widetilde{D}}=\delta-1. Since val⁡(tγ−1¯​𝔪)⊆val⁡(𝒥D)\mathrm{val}(t^{\gamma-\underline{1}}\mathfrak{m})\subseteq\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{J}_{D}), by Corollary 2.30, the equality follows. ∎

Example 4.19.

Let us consider the deformation F⁡(x,y,s1,s2)=x10+y8+s1​x5​y4+s2​x3​y6F(x,y,s_{1},s_{2})=x^{10}+y^{8}+s_{1}x^{5}y^{4}+s_{2}x^{3}y^{6} for s1,s2s_{1},s_{2} in a neighbourhood of 00 so that the deformation is equisingular. It is given in [BGM92], as an example of the stratification by the bb-function not satisfying the frontier condition.

Contrary to the previous example, this curve is not irreducible.

We notice that F⁡(x,y,s1,0)F(x,y,s_{1},0) is quasi-homogeneous. Therefore, the previous lemma shows that the values of the Jacobian ideal along the quasi-homogeneous stratum does not change. Therefore, the quasi-homogeneous stratum is a stratum of the stratification by logarithmic residues.

Moreover, one can check that there are three strata for the stratification by the Tjurina number: the quasi-homogeneous stratum S1S_{1} defined by s2=0s_{2}=0 for which τ=63\tau=63, a stratum S2S_{2} defined by s1=0s_{1}=0 and s2≠0s_{2}\neq 0 for which τ=54\tau=54 and a stratum S3S_{3} defined by s1​s2≠0s_{1}s_{2}\neq 0 for which τ=53\tau=53. Therefore, the stratification by logarithmic residues does not satisfy the frontier condition. Indeed, the stratification by logarithmic residues is finite and constructible so that there is a stratum of the stratification by logarithmic residues which is an open dense subset of S2S_{2}, which therefore contains the origin in its closure, but not the whole quasi-homogeneous stratum.

4.3. Algorithms to compute the logarithmic residues along plane curves with one or two components

We suggest here several methods which can be used to compute the values of logarithmic residues.

Thanks to the symmetry Theorem 1.2, computing the values of 𝒥D\mathscr{J}_{D} is equivalent to the computation of the values of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}.

4.3.1. Irreducible semi-quasi homogeneous polynomials

This algorithm is used to study the equisingular deformation of a quasi-homogeneous polynomial of the form xa−ybx^{a}-y^{b}, with gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a,b)=1. It is inspired by [BGM88].

We consider the following equation of an irreducible curve, with si​j∈ℂs_{ij}\in\mathbb{C} and gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a,b)=1:

(23) F⁡(x,y)=xa−yb+∑1⩽i<a−11⩽j<b−1i​b+j​a>a​bsi​j​xi​yj.F(x,y)=x^{a}-y^{b}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant i<a-1\\ 1\leqslant j<b-1\\ ib+ja>ab\end{subarray}}s_{ij}x^{i}y^{j}.

A parametrization of the curve is given by x⁡(t)=tb+g⁡(t),y⁡(t)=ta+h⁡(t)x(t)=t^{b}+g(t),y(t)=t^{a}+h(t) where g,h∈ℂ​{t}g,h\in\mathbb{C}\{t\} with val⁡(g)>b,val⁡(h)>a\mathrm{val}(g)>b,\mathrm{val}(h)>a.

We set for i,j∈ℕ2i,j\in\mathbb{N}^{2}, ρ⁡(i,j)=i​b+j​a\rho(i,j)=ib+ja. We define a monomial ordering by: (i,j)<(i′,j′)(i,j)<(i^{\prime},j^{\prime}) if and only if ρ⁡(i,j)<ρ⁡(i′,j′)\rho(i,j)<\rho(i^{\prime},j^{\prime}) or (ρ⁡(i,j)=ρ⁡(i′,j′)​ and ​i<i′)\big(\rho(i,j)=\rho(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})\text{ and }i<i^{\prime}\big). If H=∑i,jai,j​xi​yj∈ℂ⁡{x,y}H=\sum_{i,j}a_{i,j}x^{i}y^{j}\in\mathbb{C}\{x,y\} is non zero, we set exp⁡(H)=min⁡((i,j),ai,j≠0)\exp(H)=\min\left((i,j),a_{i,j}\neq 0\right) and ρ⁡(H):=ρ⁡(exp⁡(H))\rho(H):=\rho(\exp(H)).

Polynomials of the form (23) are studied in [BGM88]. The authors give an algorithm to compute the "escalier" of the curve, which is by definition the complement in ℕ2\mathbb{N}^{2} of the set

E={exp(g);g∈(F,Fx′,Fy′)⊆ℂ{x,y}}.E=\{\exp(g);g\in(F,F_{x}^{\prime},F_{y}^{\prime})\subseteq\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}\}.

More precisely, they give the explicit computation of a finite family (Aj)−1⩽j⩽K(A_{j})_{-1\leqslant j\leqslant K} of points of ℕ2\mathbb{N}^{2} such that E=⋃j=−1KAj+ℕ2E=\bigcup_{j=-1}^{K}A_{j}+\mathbb{N}^{2}, and none of the AjA_{j}’s can be removed. Then it is possible to prove:

Proposition 4.20.

We have the following equality:

val⁡(𝒥D)=⋃i=−1K(ρ⁡(Aj)+val⁡(𝒪D)).\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{J}_{D})=\bigcup_{i=-1}^{K}\Big(\rho(A_{j})+\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{O}_{D})\Big).

4.3.2. Irreducible plane curve

In [HH07], an algorithm is proposed to compute the set of values of Kähler differentials of an irreducible plane curve. By Proposition 3.32, it gives also the values of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}. In fact, one can see that the algorithm of [BGM88] corresponds to the algorithm of [HH07] by Proposition 3.31.

Moreover, if a generating family of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} is known, the algorithm of [HH07, Theorem 2.4] can be used directly on this family to compute a standard basis (H,G)(H,G) for ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D} (see [HH07, Definition 2.1]). In particular, GG is a standard basis of 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} and H⊆ℛDH\subseteq\mathscr{R}_{D}. In order to determine val⁡(ℛD)\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{R}_{D}) from HH and GG, we need the following notion:

Definition 4.21 ([HH07]).

A GG-product is an element of the form ∏i=1qgiαi\prod_{i=1}^{q}g_{i}^{\alpha_{i}} with q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}, αj∈ℕ\alpha_{j}\in\mathbb{N} and gi∈Gg_{i}\in G.

A standard basis GG of 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} is characterized by the fact that for all h∈𝒪Dh\in\mathscr{O}_{D}, there exists a GG-product gg such that val⁡(h)=val⁡(g)\mathrm{val}(h)=\mathrm{val}(g) (see [HH07]).

Example 4.22.

Let DD be the irreducible plane curve parametrized by x⁡(t)=t4x(t)=t^{4} and y⁡(t)=t6+t7y(t)=t^{6}+t^{7}. By [dJP00, Example 5.2.13], the semigroup of DD is generated by 4,6,134,6,13 so that a standard basis of 𝒪D\mathscr{O}_{D} is G={x,y,y2−x3}G=\left\{x,y,y^{2}-x^{3}\right\}. The GG-products are then the elements xi​yj​(y2−x3)kx^{i}y^{j}(y^{2}-x^{3})^{k} for i,j,k∈ℕi,j,k\in\mathbb{N}.

For any irreducible curve DD, if (H,G)(H,G) is a standard basis of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}, then:

val⁡(ℛD)={val⁡(h)+val⁡(g);h∈H,g​ a ​G​-product }.\mathrm{val}(\mathscr{R}_{D})=\left\{\mathrm{val}(h)+\mathrm{val}(g);h\in H,g\text{ a }G\text{-product }\right\}.

4.3.3. Plane curves with two branches

Let D=D1∪D2D=D_{1}\cup D_{2} be a plane curve germ with two irreducible components. We suggest here an algorithm to compute the set of negative values of ℛD\mathscr{R}_{D}. It is more technical than in the irreducible case, and cannot be generalized to plane curves with three or more branches. It can be compared to the fact that the analytic classification proposed in [HHH15] for two branches is also more complicated than in the irreducible case, and can not be easily extended to plane curves with three or more branches.

Example 4.24 illustrates the algorithm for two branches which is suggested below.
